ResNet Quantization Hands-on

From opening the OE to on-board verification

This is Lesson 3 of Chapter 2, Model Zoo: ResNet Quantization Hands-on. In the last lesson, we got a Sample running on the board, using a model that was already converted. In this lesson, we follow along and quantize ResNet-18 ourselves. We start by opening the OE, then set up the environment, write the YAML, compile, and read the complete logs. At the end, we put the artifacts back into the Sample and verify them on the board.

ResNet Quantization Hands-on · Lesson Roadmap02 / 48
This lesson follows the order of the actual operations, in four steps. Step one, open the OE: what it is, and how to get from the image into the container. Step two, set up the environment: following the conversion directory, prepare the working directory, the YAML, and the calibration data. Step three, compile: we do the X5 and the S100 once each, and show you the complete logs. Step four, look at the artifacts and the similarity, then verify on the board and run an evaluation. Before we begin, let's spend a few minutes on the PTQ theory.

RDK Classroom 2-03
Part one: let's go through the theory first.
PTQ Pipeline

The five stages of PTQ

Five PTQ stages: from the float model to on-board verification
RDK Classroom 2-03
ResNet Quantization Hands-on · Five PTQ Stages05 / 48
PTQ, post-training quantization, has five stages. One, the float model: take the weights and export them to ONNX. Two, validation: compare against PyTorch, then check the operators. Three, calibration data: prepare a batch of representative inputs. Four, quantize and compile: calibrate, quantize, and compile, once for each of the two toolchains. Five, evaluation: compare accuracy on a dataset. In this lesson, we do stage four by hand, then come back to validation and evaluation.
Input Pipeline

Preprocessing is compiled into the model

The second job: optimize, quantize, and compile into an INT8 model
RDK Classroom 2-03
ResNet Quantization Hands-on · Input Compiled In06 / 48
Conversion has to solve two things. First, how the input is handled. The board feeds the model NV12, while during training the model took RGB. Color conversion, subtracting the mean, and multiplying by a scale factor are not done on the board. Instead, they are compiled into the model at conversion time, which is exactly what mean and scale in the yaml are for. Second, optimize, quantize, and compile the model into an INT8 model that the BPU can run.
Toolchains

One ONNX, two toolchains

One ONNX, two toolchains, two kinds of artifact
RDK Classroom 2-03
ResNet Quantization Hands-on · Two Toolchains07 / 48
Both toolchains are installed in Docker images. The X5 uses hb_mapper: first checker to check the model, then makertbin to convert it. It produces a bin file; the march is bayes-e, and the input is a single packed NV12. The S series uses hb_compile, one command, and it produces an hbm file. The S100's march is nash-e, and the input is a split NV12, with Y and UV kept separate. The S100P and the S600 use the same tool and the same yaml, and we won't convert them in this lesson.

Part two: opening the OE.
What Is OE

The OE is a Docker image

S series images are on a registry; docker login before pulling
RDK Classroom 2-03
ResNet Quantization Hands-on · What the OE Is09 / 48
The OE is the algorithm toolchain provided by D-Robotics. It is not a piece of software you install, but a Docker image. The image already has all the tools needed for conversion. The X5 and the S series each have their own image versions; within a series there are also CPU images and GPU images. For PTQ alone, the CPU image is enough; when a usable GPU is available, the GPU image can speed things up. To use it, you start a container with docker run and run your commands inside. Our working directory is mounted into the container, with the same path as on the host. The artifacts we compile are written straight back to this directory, and they are still there after the container exits. The S series images are on a registry, and before pulling them you first have to docker login with your own account.

RDK Classroom 2-03
ResNet Quantization Hands-on · The X5 OE10 / 48
Let's start with the OE for the X5. The first command, docker image inspect, confirms the image is available locally. It is a v1.2.8 server image, with a name that starts with local. The first part of the output is the image's unique ID, followed by the creation time. The second command uses docker run to enter the container and runs hb_mapper with the version option. The container prints: hb_mapper 1.24.3. Then we filter pip list: hbdk 3.49.15, horizon-nn 1.1.0. With these version numbers, the versions in the later logs can be matched up. The rm, entrypoint, and bash -c in the command are explained one by one on the next page.

ResNet Quantization Hands-on · The S100 OE11 / 48
Now the image for the S100. It comes from the D-Robotics registry, with s100 in its name, version v3.7.0. This lesson's demo uses the GPU image; the same version also has a CPU image, and for PTQ the CPU image is enough. As before, first docker image inspect, then enter the container. Here's a pitfall: hb_compile does not support a version option. The command returns no such option; this is the real output, not us breaking the environment. So the version has to be read with pip list. horizon_tc_ui 3.5.3, hbdk4 4.7.5, hmct-gpu 2.6.5. The start of the compile log later prints these versions again.
docker run

docker run: one by one

① The form used in this lessonroot@rdk: ~
$ docker run --rm --entrypoint '' \
--user 1000:1000 --shm-size 15g \
-v $WORK:$WORK -w $WORK/x5 <image> \
bash -c '<command>'
Key point

With a graphics card you can add --gpus all (optional speed-up)

② What each option doesroot@rdk: ~
--rm delete on exit · --user your own files
--entrypoint '' no default entry · --shm-size shared mem
-v / -w mount and enter the working directory
--gpus all: optional with NVIDIA GPU; not needed for S series
Key point

Same path inside and outside the container; a CPU image also works

③ Going in interactivelyroot@rdk: ~
$ docker run -i -t … <image> bash
i keeps input open · t allocates a terminal
Key point

This lesson uses one-shot commands; logs are easier to save

RDK Classroom 2-03
ResNet Quantization Hands-on · docker run Options12 / 48
Let's go through the docker run parameters one by one. rm: the container is deleted when it exits, leaving no clutter. entrypoint followed by an empty string: clears the image's default entrypoint; what happens without it, you'll see on the next page. user 1000 colon 1000: run as a normal user, so the artifacts don't end up owned by root. shm-size 15g: leave the container enough shared memory. The v parameter mounts the working directory, so the host and the container see the same path. The w parameter: after the container starts, you are already in that directory. With an NVIDIA graphics card, you can add gpus all to hand the card to the container for acceleration; this is not a required parameter for the S series. The same version also has a CPU image; for PTQ the CPU image is enough, and there's no need to add gpus all. Finally, bash -c: what's in the quotes after it is the command to run. Want to go in interactively and type commands? Replace bash -c and the command after it with bash, and add the i and t parameters. i keeps the input open, and t allocates a terminal, so it feels like logging into a machine. This recording uses one-shot commands; the effect is the same, and the logs are easier to save.
Error 126

A common error: 126

① Without --entrypointroot@rdk: ~
$ docker run --rm <X5 image> bash -c 'hb_mapper checker …'
/usr/bin/bash: cannot execute binary file
EXIT_CODE=126
Key point

The default entrypoint takes bash as an argument

② With --entrypoint set to an empty stringroot@rdk: ~
$ docker run --rm --entrypoint '' <X5 image> …
→ hb_mapper starts printing its version · EXIT_CODE=0
Key point

Hit on our very first attempt

RDK Classroom 2-03
ResNet Quantization Hands-on · Error 12613 / 48
Now, a common mistake. This was our first attempt: the command had no entrypoint. The result: bash reports cannot execute binary file, exit code 126. The reason is that the image has a default entrypoint of its own, and our bash was handed to it as an argument. The fix: add entrypoint with an empty string. Run it again and it works: hb_mapper starts printing its version, exit code 0.

Next, ptq_x5.yaml, the compile configuration for the X5. The comment at the top says it clearly: these are the compile parameters used for the release artifacts. Only two placeholders, @WORK@ and @SIZE@, need to be replaced by us. work is the working directory; it appears in the model path, the working directory, and the calibration data directory. size is the input size; it appears in input_shape. ptq_s.yaml

ptq_s.yaml vs. the X5 template

Shared by S100 / S100P / S600 · @TARGET@ @MARCH@ @WORK@ @SIZE@ · 46 lines (X5: 31).

Fieldptq_x5.yamlptq_s.yaml
marchbayes-e (fixed)@MARCH@: nash-e / m / p
Default fields—debug_mode · output_nodes · remove_node_name …
Input / quant.—std_value · separate_batch · quant_config
optimize_levelO3O2
input_sourcedata: pyramidAbsent; uses a jobs / cache group instead
RDK Classroom 2-03
ResNet Quantization Hands-on · ptq_s.yaml18 / 48
Next is ptq_s.yaml, the configuration for the S series. The S100, S100P, and S600 all share this one file. The comment lists four placeholders: @TARGET@, @MARCH@, @WORK@, and @SIZE@. target is the target name; march is nash-e, nash-m, or nash-p. Compare the two templates with diff, and the differences are visible at a glance. First, the march differs: the X5 fixes bayes-e, while for the S series it is decided by a placeholder. Second, the S series has a batch of extra default-value fields, such as debug_mode and output_nodes. Third, the S series adds std_value and separate_batch, and also quant_config. Fourth, the optimization level: O3 on the X5, O2 on the S series. Fifth, the X5 has input_source, and the S series doesn't; it uses the jobs and cache group instead.

Calibration Data

Calibration data: two formats

Two targets, two formats: do not mix them up
RDK Classroom 2-03
ResNet Quantization Hands-on · Calibration Data20 / 48
Now the calibration data. The tool needs a batch of representative inputs. The Sample's recipe is fixed: 200 images. The short side is first resized to 235, then center-cropped to 224. Note that the two targets write out different data. The X5 stores the raw 0-to-255 RGB, which the loader then converts to NV12. Each one is 602,112 bytes. The S100 stores npy files that are already normalized to the ONNX input. Each one has an extra 128 bytes of file header.
Calibration Tips

Calibration matches deployment

This lesson's calibration images: one shard of the COCO dataset on Hugging Face, 200 fixed picks; not checked against the release artifacts' calibration images.

Same geometry

Resize and crop the same way as at runtime.

Same color format

X5 stores RGB first; the loader converts to NV12.

Same place for normalization

X5 normalizes inside the model; S100's data is already normalized.

RDK Classroom 2-03
ResNet Quantization Hands-on · Calibration Essentials21 / 48
The calibration data has three key points, all about matching the deployment. The geometry must match: resize and crop the same way as at runtime. The color format must match: for the X5, RGB first, then NV12. The place where normalization happens must match too. The X5's calibration data is not normalized, because the model does it internally; the S100's is already normalized. If they don't match, the quantization parameters won't be accurate. In addition, this lesson's calibration images come from one shard of COCO on Hugging Face. They were not checked against the calibration images of the release artifacts.

X5 YAML · 1/2

X5 YAML: model and input

① model_parametersroot@rdk: ~
onnx_model: /work/resnet-18/export/model.onnx
march: bayes-e
output_model_file_prefix: resnet_x5
Key point

march corresponds to the X5's BPU

② input_parametersroot@rdk: ~
input_name: data · input_layout_train: NCHW
input_type_rt: nv12
input_type_train: rgb
input_shape: 1x3x224x224
Key point

The tool compiles the color conversion into the model

③ Normalizationroot@rdk: ~
mean_value: 123.675 116.28 103.53
scale_value: 0.0171247538317 …
input_space_and_range: bt601_video
Key point

mean × 255; scale = 1 ÷ (255 × std)

RDK Classroom 2-03
ResNet Quantization Hands-on · X5 YAML (1/2)26 / 48
Now let's go through the X5's YAML section by section. First section, model_parameters: the model itself. onnx_model is the exported model.onnx; march is bayes-e, which corresponds to the X5's BPU. working_dir is the artifact output directory; output_model_file_prefix decides the file name prefix, here resnet_x5. Second section, input_parameters: how the input is handled. input_name is data, matching the ONNX input name. input_type_rt is nv12: what the board feeds the model is NV12. input_type_train is rgb: during training the model took RGB, and the tool compiles the conversion into the model. input_shape is 1x3x224x224, and the layout is NCHW. norm_type uses data_mean_and_scale: subtract the mean first, then multiply by the scale. mean_value is the ImageNet mean times 255; scale_value is 1 divided by 255 times the standard deviation. input_space_and_range is bt601_video, which corresponds to the limited range of NV12.
X5 YAML · 2/2

X5 YAML: calibration and compile

④ calibration_parametersroot@rdk: ~
cal_data_dir: /work/resnet-18/x5/calibration/data
cal_data_type: float32
calibration_type: default
preprocess_on: false
Key point

default = automatic search

⑤ compiler_parametersroot@rdk: ~
optimize_level: O3
compile_mode: latency
core_num: 1
input_source:
data: pyramid
Key point

pyramid: the input comes from the board's NV12 path

RDK Classroom 2-03
ResNet Quantization Hands-on · X5 YAML (2/2)27 / 48
Third section, calibration_parameters: calibration. cal_data_dir points to the 200 files we prepared. cal_data_type is float32, matching the rgb files. calibration_type is set to default, which means automatic search; an animation later explains it. preprocess_on is false: the data is already prepared, so the tool doesn't need to process the images. Fourth section, compiler_parameters: compilation. optimize_level is O3; the larger the number, the more optimization. compile_mode is latency, aiming for low latency. core_num is 1, so it uses only one core. In input_source, data is set to pyramid: the input comes from the board's NV12 image path. Put the four sections together, and you have a complete conversion configuration.
Calibration Search

default means automatic search

Same setting, but the chosen method can differ
RDK Classroom 2-03
ResNet Quantization Hands-on · Calibration Methods28 / 48
In the yaml, calibration_type is written as default. This isn't doing nothing; it is an automatic search. The tool tries a set of candidates. The target similarity is 0.995. Candidate one: two methods, max or kl. Candidate two: the percentile, 0.99995 or 1.0. Candidate three: per_channel and asymmetric, each tried on and off. The results differ: the X5 chose max-percentile, with percentile 0.99995. The S100 chose kl, with num_bin 1024. With the same setting, the chosen method can be different. The details are left for the next lesson.
S100 YAML

The S100's YAML: how it differs from the X5's

Cosine Similarity

How to read similarity

Below 0.8 usually means obvious accuracy loss; only a reference, task accuracy decides
RDK Classroom 2-03
ResNet Quantization Hands-on · Reading Similarity36 / 48
After conversion, look at the similarity first. The S100 log has two columns. Calibrated is the cosine between the float model and the calibrated model: 0.999913. Quantized is the cosine between the float model and the quantized fixed-point model: 0.999856. The X5 has only one column. It is the cosine between the float model and the quantized model: 0.999941. The two sides use different definitions, so don't compare which is better. An output-node similarity below 0.8 usually means an obvious accuracy loss. It is only a reference; in the end, what counts is the task accuracy.

Evaluation Pipeline

How evaluation works

On the board, evaluate_board.py evaluates the bin or hbm
RDK Classroom 2-03
ResNet Quantization Hands-on · How Evaluation Works43 / 48
Stage five, evaluation. Evaluation means comparing accuracy on a dataset, and the pipeline has five steps: data, preprocessing, model, take the top few, and statistics. The data is the MatchedFrequency set of ImageNetV2: ten thousand images, one thousand classes. Note that it is not the ILSVRC 2012 validation set, so the numbers cannot be compared with that set's. Preprocessing is resize and crop to 224, with the same rule on both paths. The model gives one thousand scores, which are sorted to take the top five. If the first place equals the label, it counts as Top-1 correct; if the label is among the top five, it counts as Top-5 correct. The statistic is the proportion of correct images out of the total. On the PC, evaluate.py evaluates the float ONNX. On the board, evaluate_board.py evaluates the bin or hbm.

Rules

The five rules of conversion

When it will not run, or the numbers do not match, check these five first.

  • 1The image needs --entrypoint ''
  • 2PTQ runs on the CPU alone; a GPU is only an optional speed-up; CUDA messages in the log can be ignored
  • 3Calibration preprocessing must match deployment
  • 4Switching board types means converting again (S100P uses nash-m)
  • 5Verify with Top-1 and the order of magnitude of the scores
RDK Classroom 2-03
ResNet Quantization Hands-on · Five Rules46 / 48
Finally, five rules. One, the image needs an empty entrypoint, otherwise you get 126. Two, PTQ can be done on the CPU alone, and the GPU is only an optional speed-up; the CUDA messages in the log can be ignored. Three, the calibration preprocessing must match the deployment. Four, artifacts are compiled per board type, and switching board types means converting again. The S100P needs a separate conversion with nash-m. Five, for verification, look at Top-1 and the order of magnitude of the scores.
